item.title: New poll suggests gloomy GOP outlook for midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump’s sinking ratings threaten to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, as voters blame him for high prices and a shaky economy, according to a new NBC News poll . The president’s approval rating stands at 41% among registered voters, a second-term low in the poll, with a majority (55%) of voters saying they believe Trump’s policies have hurt the economy. That’s up from 48% in March, before the Iran war pushed up prices on gas and other goods and cemented the rising cost of living as voters’ most pressing issue. NBC News Democrats hold a 5-point edge in the battle for control of Congress, 50%-45% — not nearly as large a lead as the 12-point advantage the party enjoyed at this point before the 2018 election, when Democrats rode an anti-Trump wave to the House majority in his first midterm as president. Despite that lead, the Democratic Party is still viewed more negatively than Trump and the GOP. That could help Republicans, along with the fact that the fight for control of the House and especially the Senate is playing out in traditionally Republican parts of the country. Democrats would have to flip multiple states Trump carried by double digits in 2024 to win the Senate. NBC News “We have a classic battle between these numbers and the political geography in which this campaign will be decided,” said Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies, whose firm conducted the survey alongside Democratic firm Hart Research Associates. “And the Republicans are still standing because of the geography in which this election will be won or lost.” Still, the poll suggests an increasingly gloomy political environment for the GOP. Longtime double-digit leads over the Democratic Party on who would better handle inflation and the economy have evaporated. More than 6 in 10 voters say the Iran war has not been worth it. Voters don’t appear to be motivated by Trump’s signature tax and spending legislation he championed last year. Instead, Trump himself is a powerful motivating factor, but more for Democrats than for Republicans, as more voters — including nearly half of independents — say they consider their vote a signal of opposition to the president than at any other time in three decades of NBC News polling before midterm elections. “Donald Trump has achieved his goal of making this election about him at a historic level. The problem for Trump and Republicans on the ballot in November is that he has also made history in the highest share of voters who say their vote is in opposition to Trump,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates. Republicans on the campaign trail are trying to shore up their standing by arguing that Democrats are too extreme to trust with congressional majorities. But the poll indicates voters are more anxious about restraining Trump: 50% say they’re more concerned that Republicans will go too far in supporting Trump if they keep control of Congress, while 42% are more concerned Democrats will obstruct the president if they win control of Congress. Independents lean 45%-30% toward greater concern that Republicans will go too far supporting Trump. McInturff acknowledged the challenges for the GOP posed by the political environment, even as the party’s geographic advantages keep Democrats fighting on their turf. “The issue environment is tilting substantially towards the Democrats,” McInturff said. Trump’s struggles continue A majority of voters, 56%, disapprove of Trump’s job performance, including overwhelming shares of Democrats and independents and 16% of Republicans. The share of voters who strongly approve of Trump, 25%, is the second-lowest mark recorded in the NBC News poll across Trump’s first and second terms. The disapproval rating closely tracks the 55% who say Trump’s policies have hurt the economy, while 26% say they have helped and 18% say they have not made much of a difference. At this point in the 2018 election cycle, more voters said Trump’s policies helped the economy (41%) than hurt (26%). And the survey suggests some of Trump’s signature economic policies are falling flat. While Republicans are touting Trump’s signature tax cut and spending measure known as the “big, beautiful bill,” which was enacted in 2025, 42% of voters say they are less likely to support a candidate backing the measure, while 36% say they are more likely to support such a candidate. Trump’s latest gambit — an announcement at the recent Republican convention that he wanted to issue $5,000 payments to every adult if Republicans keep control of Congress — isn’t garnering much interest. While 21% of voters say they’re more likely to back a candidate who supports Trump’s plan, 46% say they’d be less likely. A plurality of Republicans say it would make no difference in their vote choice, while Democrats are uniformly against the idea and 45% of independents would be less likely to support a candidate in favor of the plan. Among independents, 13% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate who backs Trump’s plan. Voters are also continuing to express opposition to the Iran war, with 57% saying they are less likely to support a candidate who supports the war, versus 24% who are more likely to support that candidate. One-third of voters say the war has been worth it, while 62% disagree. And Democrats also have a 4-point advantage, within the poll’s margin of error, on the question of which party voters say they trust to handle the war with Iran. Trump has continued to insert himself into the midterms, including endorsing nearly all Republicans in competitive congressional races. But 52% of voters are less likely to support a candidate endorsed by Trump, while 30% are more likely to support a Trump-backed candidate. Democratic opportunities — and challenges Clear dissatisfaction with the president opens the door for Democrats as they fight for control of Congress this fall. Forty-three percent of registered voters say their vote for Congress is intended to signal opposition to Trump, while 27% say they plan to vote to send a signal of support for Trump and 28% say their vote won’t be a signal either way. Among independents, almost half (46%) see their vote as a signal of opposition to Trump, while just a handful (10%) say their vote is a signal of support for the president. Democrats have a 1-point lead when voters are asked which party they trust more in dealing with the economy — a result within the poll’s margin of error. It’s the third consecutive NBC News poll with both parties sitting about even on that question. In the same survey just three years ago, Republicans enjoyed a 21-point advantage when it came to handling the economy. Democrats also have a 7-point edge on controlling inflation, as well as slight leads on dealing with the war in Iran and dealing with corruption — government corruption was the second-most popular choice when voters were asked to rank the most important issue facing the country, with concern about the issue heightened among members of both parties and independents. The Democratic Party also has double-digit leads on dealing with data centers and dealing with healthcare. Republicans still hold significant advantages over Democrats on handling crime, border security and immigration, including a 21-point lead on border security. But that is down from the 36-point edge the GOP held over Democrats on the issue in Sept. 2022, after Trump has made aggressive immigration enforcement a hallmark of his second term. Democrats also have a narrow lead on interest in the election, as well as among party identification. But it’s not all rosy for the opposition party. The Republican Party is viewed more positively by voters: 36% have a positive view of the GOP, while 49% view the party negatively. On the Democratic Party, voters are split 29%-50%. Meanwhile, the Democratic Socialists of America is viewed positively by 22% of voters, as Republicans try to link other Democrats to the left-wing group, which rose in prominence following some major primary wins in the past two years. One poll respondent — Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old Texan who doesn’t affiliate with either party — told NBC News that he hasn’t plugged into the election yet and is still unsure whom he’ll vote for. But he said his father grew up during the Cold War and that he’s wary of Democrats who describe themselves as democratic socialists. “Any relation toward socialism or communism in general gives me the ick. It’s like a buzzword that generally just makes me not want to sway in that direction,” he said. Half of voters say they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who “supports many of the Democratic Socialists of America’s proposed policies,” while 31% say they’d be more likely to support those kinds of candidates. Candidates calling to abolish ICE, a big point of emphasis among progressives, draw similarly unpopular scores with voters. That said, for all the Democratic infighting over policies like “Medicare for All,” 53% of voters say they would be more likely to support a candidate who favors the policy, while 36% said it would make them less likely to vote for that candidate. When asked a similar question with slightly different wording to note the healthcare would be financed in part by taxes, 49% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate that backed the policy and 39% say they’d be less likely. Horwitt, the Democratic pollster, noted that his party “remains in a terrible position as a brand nationally,” even as the poll paints a dismal picture for Trump and Republicans. “This speaks more to deep dissatisfaction with Trump and Republicans than a ringing endorsement of Democrats,” he said. “The party in power does not have a positive story to tell on the major issues of the day: inflation, corruption and the Iran war. Voters are continuing to look for change.” The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Sept. 11-15 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. item.title: Obama rips White House's approach to AI after Trump dubbed security fears a 'hoax'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Former President Obama on Friday slammed President Trump over his handling of how to approach artificial intelligence amid "doomsday" warnings coming from some in the tech industry about the technology's potential existential threat to humanity. Obama said during an interview at Colgate University in New York that the federal government must regulate AI, before referring to comments made by one Trump adviser. "I heard one of Donald Trump’s main advisers on this make the argument that, 'The market will take care of AI,'" the former president said. "'These companies will solve the safety issues because they have every incentive to do so — if it turns out to be dangerous, people will just sue them, and they’re worried about financial liability.'" "That’s not how we treat airlines," Obama added. "Or drug companies, or food companies." Obama continued to say that AI could become a threat at a human level if it falls into the clutches of "bad humans" and if self-improving AI models realize they no longer need humans. He referred to Trump again in that his successor has said regulations on AI are "for losers." "So we’ve got a gap of at least a couple of years where things are moving really fast and we have an administration that is not capable of or willing to — I would argue both — putting together a serious regulatory framework," Obama said. He emphasized "encouraging some sort of voluntary industry restraint" as the "best we can do now" until both the legislative and executive branches "start getting serious about this." Obama has reportedly urged House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to make AI oversight a central tenet of his caucus’s agenda. The New York Times reported the former president told Jeffries at a fundraiser that AI could be "dangerous" without congressional oversight. On Saturday, Trump announced that he will develop an "AI Force" and appoint a "czar" to oversee AI development, though he said in his announcement that any concerns surrounding a lack of federal AI guardrails were a "hoax." The president also suggested that AI be renamed to "Superior Intelligence," "Extreme Intelligence" and "Supreme Intelligence," which he said were "far more elegant and accurate description[s] of this new phenomena." Trump notably opposed the Obama administration's history of imposing regulations during his first run for president. Bipartisan lawmakers have raised the alarm on AI development after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon recently warned that the technology " could kill us all " by the end of the decade. Some lawmakers, namely Rep. George Whitesides (D-Calif.), have called for a slowdown to develop red lines on AI to allow Congress to step in and turn those red lines into law. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's head of alignment, affirmed that Coxon was "correct" in that "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans !" Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei weighed in last Saturday, saying that development must slow down to allow for the implementation of necessary risk prevention safeguards. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. item.title: Iran and U.S. trade threats after Houthi attacks escalate regional conflict.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jana Choukeir and Doina Chiacu DUBAI/WASHINGTON, Sept 20 (Reuters) - Iran and the United States exchanged new threats on Sunday, with President Donald Trump warning Iran would fail economically or face its leadership being wiped out if it didn't make a deal, and the Iranian ‌military saying it would retaliate harshly to any fresh attack. The conflict has looked stalemated for months, with no sign either side was ready ‌for concessions even as it has deepened a global energy crisis, cratered swathes of Iran's economy and spilled over into new regional escalations. In a phone call with a Fox News reporter, Trump ​said Iran's leaders should make a deal, rot economically or be wiped out, the reporter said. However, with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly, Trump said he would be open to meeting him, the Fox reporter added. Trump has repeatedly made vague threats of major military escalations during the conflict that began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28, without carrying them out. Earlier, Iran's military central command said any new attack would trigger sustained ‌retaliation against US bases and interests and that Washington's ⁠regional allies would be considered parties to the conflict. The Iranian military added that it had information that an attack was being prepared, without elaborating on what that information might be. HOUTHIS TARGET RIYADH US Gulf allies have already been badly scarred by a ⁠war that the US and Israel launched with no warning, bringing their cities under Iranian fire and hammering their economies with the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway blockaded. On Saturday their predicament worsened further, with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi group launching missile and drone strikes at the Saudi capital after having made sudden military gains in Yemen's reignited civil war ​earlier ​this month. Reuters video showed a massive plume of black smoke billowing from the area of ​Riyadh's main international airport following booms overnight. The US State Department ‌issued a security alert citing the Houthi hostilities. It said there was potential for unforeseen escalation in the Middle East, and Americans should exercise more vigilance and be aware of possible flight cancellations and airspace closures. Saudi Arabia did not comment on the incident, though a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had foiled other attacks on the kingdom. Recent escalation by the Houthis has forced Riyadh into a painful dilemma: continue airstrikes on the group to stop it seizing more Yemeni territory or step back in the hopes of averting drone strikes on critical infrastructure. ENERGY EXPORTS BLOCKADED The Houthi gains along the coast mean the group's forces ‌now sit on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, giving them easier control over shipping travelling between ​the Red Sea and Asia and the ability to blockade the crucial waterway. With Iran already ​having blockaded most shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the oil-rich Gulf's ​energy exports are now almost entirely cut off from global markets, adding to pressure on oil prices. A US blockade of ‌Iranian ports is meanwhile stopping Iran from selling its own oil, ​contributing to major problems in the Islamic ​Republic's economy. Despite the economic damage, there is little sign of a return to the interim ceasefire agreement that was struck in June but fell apart in July amid disputes over its terms. Iran reiterated on Sunday that it would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the terms ​of that June agreement, as it interpreted them, were met. Iranian ‌Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said Iran would have to keep on fighting as well as negotiating, to push back its enemies ​and to consolidate any gains with diplomacy. (Reporting by Jana Choukeir in Dubai and Doina Chiacu in Washington; Additional reporting by Timour Azhari ​in Riyadh; Writing by Angus McDowall; Editing by Aidan Lewis and Ros Russell) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/iran-warns-against-escalation-us-131851523.html

item.title: Russia lured Ukrainian teens to launch attacks. Now they're in prison.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
KREMENCHUK, Ukraine - Yaroslav Suzanskyi was 16 when he saw an ad on the Telegram messaging app offering “easy money,” about $165, to do an odd job. It turned out to be a want-ad for sabotage: Suzanskyi was paid to set fire to a railway relay cabinet. Now 18, Suzanskyi is incarcerated at a juvenile correctional colony, both a perpetrator and a victim of a hidden part of Russia’s war against Ukraine: recruiting vulnerable young people to attack their own country. He is one of eight inmates at Kremenchuk - in a population of 72 - convicted of national security or public safety offenses linked to Russia. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Many of the children recruited by Russia are impoverished and are lured into betraying Ukraine with relatively small offers of money, the authorities said. After torching the railway equipment, Suzanskyi got a bigger offer involving an explosive, for 60,000 hryvnias, or about $1,430. A man Suzanskyi knew as Artem sent him to a hotel in the Kyiv suburbs, where two backpacks were left outside Suzanskyi’s room. One contained military clothing, the other a taped box with wires that Suzanskyi thought was a jammer but later learned was an explosive device. He was then sent by taxi to a library. Ukrainian intelligence officers intercepted him there before he could complete the assignment. “Those 60,000 turned into five years,” Suzanskyi said. Suzanskyi was 13 when Russia’s full-scale invasion began. His father and stepfather were drafted, leaving his mother to support three children. A bureaucratic mistake stopped the family’s child-support payments, and they fell behind on bills, he said. He began taking whatever work he could find. In December 2024, with his younger brother’s birthday and the winter holidays approaching, Suzanskyi said he had just 200 hryvnias, or about $5, left. That’s when he responded to the ad on Telegram. Across Ukraine, 13 minors are serving sentences in Russia-related cases, including five girls, according to the Justice Ministry. In all, more than 300 juveniles have been detained on similar charges, officials said. Some received probation, while others are still under investigation. A report published last year by the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights noted “a surge in credible allegations that the Russian Federation used Ukrainian children in Government-controlled territory to conduct surveillance and transmit information on the Ukrainian military, or to commit sabotage and arson targeting military objects or public property with links to the military.” Russia denies the allegations and has blamed Ukrainian intelligence services for recruiting Russian minors to carry out sabotage in Russia. Oleksii Babakov, now 17, spent about eight months under Russian occupation in Vovchansk, on the Russian border, where he was living in foster care. When he was 15, guardians helped get him to Kharkiv and eventually to live in Poland, which is when he saw a Telegram ad promising easy money. Babakov was asked to recruit other young people and pass them on to a handler. One was Vikentii, now also 17, a friend of Babakov’s from when they attended a cadet corps together in Kharkiv in 2022. Vikentii spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his first name because of fear that he will be targeted for retaliation. Babakov told him that he could earn up to $3,000 a month. At first, Vikentii said, he thought he would only have to make explosive devices. Later, he learned that he was also expected to plant one. He was 15 at the time. He left the device in a trash bin outside a police station in Kharkiv and walked away. “When I blew up the bomb, I understood that I had done a really bad thing,” he said. He later saw a report that no one had been hurt. “I felt relieved,” he said. “There’d been a terrorist attack, but no one was hurt.” From Poland, Babakov saw news reports about people he had recruited. One was Vikentii. Another was a 15-year-old girl who left an explosive device outside a different police station. No one was hurt in that blast either. Ukrainian authorities tracked down Babakov in Poland, and he was deported to Ukraine. He and Vikentii met again in a pretrial detention center and are now serving their sentences together in Kremenchuk. Vikentii was convicted of committing a terrorist act and sentenced to three years in prison. Babakov was convicted of inciting and assisting a terrorist attack and sentenced to four years. Maksym Parshyn, 17, is from Slovyansk, in the eastern region of Donetsk that Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to surrender. Parshyn’s mother has schizophrenia, and his family has struggled financially. Parshyn said legitimate employers were reluctant to hire him because he was too young. For a while, he loaded firewood and worked for illegal call centers scamming people in Russia. “It’s very easy,” Parshyn said of finding work on Telegram. “You write something like ‘find work,’ and it’s all there.” Parshyn accepted $300 from an anonymous Telegram contact he described as a “handler” to set fire to a railway relay cabinet. The next day, the same contact offered him more money to burn vehicles used by military recruitment officers. Parshyn said he refused and blocked the account. A few weeks later, however, he accepted another offer to spray-paint graffiti on a military recruitment office. Months later, he returned to Telegram where a new handler had offered him $3,000 to set fire to a post office. Parshyn filmed while one of his friends set the fire. Parshyn said he did not realize until he was detained that Russian intelligence services were using Telegram to recruit young Ukrainians for such attacks. He spent about a year in pretrial detention before being sentenced to four years. “I needed money,” Parshyn said. “If I hadn’t needed it, I wouldn’t have done it at all.” After turning 18, teenagers can remain in Kremenchuk for education and rehabilitation until age 22 or they may be transferred to adult facilities. Deputy Justice Minister Yevhen Pikalov said the boys detained in Kremenchuk were motivated by money not treason. “They did not do it with the motive of destroying the Ukrainian state,” Pikalov said. “They didn’t do it because they love Russia. $500 on Telegram, that’s it.” In the colony, personal phones are not allowed. Staff hold the boys’ SIM cards, and calls and video calls go through the institution. Computers and tablets are supervised, and social media is blocked. During free time, the boys play sports, read, watch television or use a PlayStation. Money from family or earned inside the facility can be spent at the colony shop. In Kremenchuk, as everywhere in Ukraine, life is overshadowed by Russian airstrikes. Blast waves from nearby missile attacks have damaged the colony three times, but the detainees were in shelters, and no one was hurt, staff said. Air-raid alerts frequently interrupt classes at the school. When The Washington Post visited on July 20, one room, normally used for table tennis, was set up for Ukraine’s university entrance exam the next day. In another, chess and checkers boards came out. A few sat down to play while others chatted. A key question for all of the boys is: What comes next? Pikalov said that judging whether a youth has been rehabilitated depends on each teenager’s risks and needs rather than the offense they committed. Babakov dreams of a “clean slate.” Parshyn said he wants to hug his family after getting out. For Suzanskyi, that next step has already begun. He has started an online university degree in agronomy. After turning 18 in June, Suzanskyi chose to transfer to a more restrictive medium-security prison for adult men, rather than remain in Kremenchuk. “To try adult life,” he said, “so I definitely won’t want to end up in prison again.” On Aug. 11, he left Kremenchuk. With 3½ years still to serve, what worries him most is what might happen to his family as Russian attacks intensify. “I’m afraid there simply won’t be any relatives left by the time I get out,” he said. item.title: Over a dozen states are closer than ever to making daylight saving time permanent
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(NEXSTAR) – The days getting shorter serve as a reminder that we're barreling toward the end of our seasonal observation of daylight saving time, but the wheels may be in motion to stop that – a move more than a dozen states have been waiting to happen. Earlier this year, the House passed the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent throughout the U.S. , with few exceptions. It's been held up in the Senate since July but, now that the chamber has returned from recess, there's a chance the legislation could be picked up. If it can pass the Senate, the bill seems to stand a fair chance of becoming law, with President Trump already expressing support . No more sunsets before 5 p.m.? How permanent daylight saving would change winter For more than a dozen states, this is the closest they've been in years to seeing some of their own legislation finally take effect. The U.S. hasn't been this close to permanent daylight saving time since a version of the Sunshine Protection Act passed in the Senate in 2022 but fizzled in the House. At present, states are only allowed to opt into year-round permanent standard time , as Hawaii and much of Arizona have done . But that hasn't stopped 19 states from enacting legislation that would make daylight saving time permanent in their jurisdiction, pending approval from Congress. In 2018, Florida became the first state to call for year-round DST . It's congressional lawmakers from the Sunshine State who have spearheaded several attempts to make daylight saving time permanent in the U.S., including the version of the Sunshine Protection Act passed by the House this year. Last year, Maine and Texas became the latest states to approve year-round daylight saving time legislation. Several of the states that have enacted similar legislation within the past eight years have stipulations in their bills that further rely on their neighbors locking their clocks. Delaware, for example, followed Florida's lead but said that Maryland, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania must also make daylight saving time permanent. None of them have, though bills to do so in New Jersey and Pennsylvania remain alive. ‘Super’ El Niño is now a near certainty. Here are 5 side effects you may not know about Colorado , Wyoming, Utah , Montana , Idaho , and Washington have similar requirements within their enacted legislation. Oregon (Malheur County would be excluded) has enacted legislation as well, but awaits action by California. Voters there gave their legislators the OK to lock the clocks in 2018, but the state has failed to do so. Other states to enact all-year daylight saving time legislation are Alabama , Georgia, Louisiana, Minnesota , Mississippi , Oklahoma , South Carolina , and Tennessee. States that tried, and failed, to make daylight saving time permanent this year include Alaska, Illinois, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Virginia, and West Virginia, according to legislative tracking by Nexstar. Meanwhile, several states tried to make standard time permanent this year, but also failed (legislation in Michigan , New Jersey , and Pennsylvania remains alive). States can still opt to lock their clocks on permanent standard time under the Sunshine Protection Act. For now, though, no clocks are locking on daylight saving time. It's not clear if or when the Senate could take up the Sunshine Protection Act or if it has enough votes to pass and make daylight saving time permanent. NEW YORK (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday the U.S. has proposed a new “notification mechanism” for artificial intelligence incidents that could affect national security, part of weekend discussions ahead of talks at the White House this week between President Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping . “We want a shared vision of common goals and common threats,” Bessent told reporters after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York. “We think that just like any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important.” Trump has resisted calls to slow down AI development , saying that would help China catch up to U.S. companies. Standing together in the soaring lobby of the JPMorgan Chase headquarters late Sunday, Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the groundwork had been laid for talks between Xi and Trump set to take place on Thursday. They said the two sides had agreed to operationalize a new “Board of Trade” that the two leaders had discussed when they met in Beijing in May. “Today those notions have become reality,” Greer said. Greer said the countries were still discussing what “nonsensitive” items could be considered for lower tariffs, but that the list could potentially include consumer and agricultural goods, energy products and medical devices. Chinese state media Xinhua said Bessent and the vice premier talked about issues “relating to AI” without mentioning specifics and also had “candid, in-depth and constructive” discussions on key economic and trade issues. “The fact that both sides agreed to continue the dialogue is significant,” said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group consultancy, in written comments. “The initial outcome — an AI risk notification mechanism — sets a precedent that other countries may follow.” ___ Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong and Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report. item.title: 'He died in my arms': Patrick Clancy opens up about the grief of losing 3 children
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Patrick Clancy said he felt he had no purpose after his three children were killed. "There was a time where I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday," Clancy, 36, said in an interview with 60 Minutes. "And I was completely fine with it." His interview with correspondent Ross Douthat comes after his ex-wife's mistrial earlier this month. The court has yet to determine whether Patrick's ex-wife, Lindsay Clancy, will be retried for the killings of their children: 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. It also comes as Patrick and his wife, Rachel Danis, face intense public scrutiny, becoming the subjects of online suspicion and speculation on social media. What happened after Callan was born In October 2022, five months after Callan's birth, Patrick said Lindsay told him she had gone a few nights without sleeping. Over the next two months, Lindsay made repeated emergency room visits. She admitted herself to a program for patients with postpartum depression and was discharged after a day of treatment. Lindsay was also prescribed an escalating number of prescription drugs. Patrick said he struggled to help his wife navigate the medical system and did not know how to manage a postpartum illness. "I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive," he said. December was the low point, Patrick said. "It was a big struggle for her — just a huge lack of sleep, deep, deep depression, intrusive thoughts." Lindsay checked herself into McLean Psychiatric Hospital on New Year's Eve. She was treated for depression and released days later, making it home in time to celebrate Cora's birthday on Jan. 7. The deaths of Cora, Dawson and Callan Less than three weeks later, Patrick said he came home from an errand to find Lindsay lying in the backyard, her throat and wrists cut, paralyzed after jumping from an upstairs window. He said he found his children strangled in the basement. Cora and Dawson were dead. Callan was airlifted to Boston Children's Hospital. "I really thought there was a chance that Callan would live," Patrick recalled. "I remember just thinking, 'Just give me one. Just give me one kid, and I would raise him as best I could, and I would give him the best life I possibly could. I'd tell him about his brother and sister.' And I was holding out hope for that." Callan's heart kept beating for four days. "I got to hold him. I got to lay down next to him. And he died in my arms," Patrick said. Patrick Clancy forgives his ex-wife In the days after the tragedy, Patrick wrote tributes to each of his three children and decided to publicly forgive Lindsay. "I saw headlines that said, you know, 'Killer Mom,' and 'Baby Murderer,' 'Monster.' And none of them were accurate," Patrick said. "I think if people said, 'She did a horrible thing,' I think everyone could agree with that. …But I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that." So I shared those words." Lindsay never asked for forgiveness, but Patrick said he gave it to her. They've both brought medical malpractice lawsuits against health care providers who treated Lindsay. Some have denied wrongdoing, and others have yet to respond to the claim. Patrick said he thinks he "did the best I could with what I had at the time. And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day." Patrick said he realized he could no longer stay in Duxbury and moved to New York City that April, seeking anonymity. Trial in court — and in the court of public opinion In July, Lindsay Clancy's trial began. Her lawyers argued she was suffering from dangerous postpartum psychosis and couldn't be held criminally responsible for her actions. The trial became a national obsession – generating furious arguments about the relationship between mental illness and criminal fault, how the medical system fails mothers and how men and women understand one another. Patrick testified and found himself at the center of an online swarm of sleuths and influencers dissecting every detail of the case, developing theories that portray him as uncaring, unfaithful and even the murderer of his children. "It's painful to see. And it makes it difficult to be in public and it's possible that some of those people, after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it and that's what we're left with," he said. One of the catalysts for the theories about Patrick was his apparent stoicism on the witness stand. Patrick said that testifying was difficult for him and that he had a "massive, traumatic" panic attack on the second day of his testimony. "They put me in an ambulance," Patrick said. "They offered me some medication, but I said, 'I don't want it, because I want to go back and I want to finish this so I can be done with this.' And I went back and I finished the testimony." Lindsay's trial ended with a hung jury earlier this month. Moving forward Patrick says reaching out to survivors and experts in the field of postpartum health has helped him move forward. He remarried this April to Dr. Rachel Danis, a fertility doctor in New York City. Danis said the pair met in January 2024 in a New York City run club and got to know each other over coffee. "Pat pulled out his phone to pay, and I noticed this adorable photo of children as the wallpaper," Danis said. " I just asked, 'Who are those cuties?' And Pat said, 'Those are my kids.' And then I think I asked if they live in Massachusetts, and Pat said, 'They died.' And this is just at the cashier." Danis said she tried to "take some of the weight from Pat." "I can't bring his kids back," she said. "But if I can honor them and allow Pat to grieve but also just continue to honor them in the present, it, I guess that's all I can do." The pair are starting a family, and Patrick is preparing to one day tell his future child about their older siblings, Cora, Dawson and Callan. "I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids," he said. "And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister." item.title: ICE agent shoots and wounds man in Austin, authorities say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man Sunday afternoon in Austin, Texas, local authorities said, and anti-ICE protesters quickly gathered at the scene. The man was in serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on the capital city's north side, Austin officials said at a news conference. The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not participate in the news conference and didn’t respond to repeated requests for details. City police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, which occurred after a traffic stop, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said while briefing reporters along with the city's mayor and other officials. Mayor says he wants city's police involved in investigation Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said he wants the city's police department to have a role in the investigation so it can provide “clear, third-party eyes” in the process. Watson said he does not think it would be appropriate for ICE to conduct an investigation on its own. Austin residents have “a right to feel safe in their city,” Watson said. A proper investigation will only enhance credibility, he added. The chief said there were not many facts she could provide so soon after the incident but added that her department’s special investigation unit was at the scene. The Texas Department of Public Safety said it received a request from ICE for assistance in a vehicle pursuit around 12:50 p.m. By the time DPS troopers arrived, the shooting had already taken place, the department said in a statement Sunday evening. Attorney says man shot is from Venezuela An immigration attorney representing the man’s family identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan man. Attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch said in a video posted to her Instagram account that she believed he had no criminal history and no final order of removal from the U.S., but she later told The Associated Press that she did not know his current immigration status. The man’s family has struggled to get any information from the hospital about his status or location, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. Just before 7 p.m., the man’s wife was informed by the hospital’s attorney that the man had been released into ICE custody a few hours earlier, Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote in a text to AP. “No one bothered to update her,” she wrote. It wasn’t immediately clear if the man remained hospitalized while in ICE custody or if he had been transferred elsewhere. Protesters turn out at the scene A dark blue Toyota Corolla was parked under an overpass with damage to its passenger-side door and what appeared to be bullet holes. The car was towed away in the early evening and traffic began moving again. A large law enforcement presence was present along with a crowd of about a hundred protesters. Some demonstrators cursed at police officers holding riot shields, while others yelled out as passing cars honked in support of the protest. One man held a sign saying, “Nobody is safe” and, on the other side, “ICE Nazi.” Asked if Austin authorities knew where the involved federal agent is, given that agents have left states after previous shootings nationwide, the mayor said: “We do not know that. But my hope would be that, an agent that’s involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city. Certainly not leave the state.” The office of Travis County District Attorney José Pompa Garza asked that local police and prosecutors be included in the investigation. “We further request cooperation from the federal government in giving us access to the evidence,” the DA's office said in a statement Sunday evening. U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, called for transparency as the shooting is investigated. “It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep,” Casar told reporters. “For Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here.” ICE enforcement operations surged around the nation over the summer The shooting comes as ICE surges enforcement across the country this summer, producing more than 50,000 arrests a month for the first time in its history in July and August. In July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, of Houston, after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site. Also in July, 25-year-old Johan Sebastián, a Colombian man, was shot by an ICE officer in Maine . The officer is an Army veteran who has struggled with serious mental health issues since early childhood and never should have been given a badge and gun to patrol American streets, several of his close relatives told AP. The administration’s enforcement efforts were widely condemned last winter after the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota. ___ Weber reported from Los Angeles and Boone from Boise, Idaho. Contributing were Associated Press journalists Kimberlee Kruesi in Providence, Rhode Island and Tim Sullivan in Minneapolis. item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen. Bill Cassidy (Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) Sen. Bill Cassidy on Sunday called on President Donald Trump to provide evidence for his claims about childhood vaccines, warning that discouraging immunization could result in more illnesses, hospitalizations, and deaths. The Louisiana Republican, a physician and chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, told CBS' "Face the Nation" that Trump should explain the basis for his proposal to split some childhood vaccines into multiple doses. "There needs to be, though, radical honesty," Cassidy said. "Have the president come forward. What is he basing this on? Who's giving him advice?" Trump said Friday that he would demand that drug companies split up children's vaccines into five doses, saying the change would lead to "a massive reduction in autism." Cassidy said he did not know which vaccines Trump was referring to or where the proposal originated. "If you want to be radically honest, the vaccines are safe," Cassidy said. "They've been proven to be safe." Cassidy warned that Trump's comments could have consequences because Americans listen to the president. "If he discourages immunization, there'll be fewer people immunized, and if we're speaking of measles, there'll be more people sick, in the hospital or even die," Cassidy said. Cassidy also said Heidi Overton, Trump's nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, would need to demonstrate at her confirmation hearing that she rejects Trump's characterization of the measles vaccine as lethal. "I need to hear that she understands that calling the measles vaccine lethal is absurd," Cassidy said. Cassidy pointed to recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania and a measles exposure at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia as evidence of the risks posed by the disease. "The president should be saying, 'Be vaccinated. It is safe and effective,'" Cassidy said. Asked whether the administration's vaccine messaging could hurt Republicans in the midterm elections, Cassidy cited polling showing strong support for childhood vaccination among women and said confusing public health messaging "probably does hurt." Cassidy also criticized Trump's proposal to provide $5,000 payments to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress in the midterm elections, calling the plan inflationary. "It's absolutely inflationary," Cassidy said. "If Joe Biden had proposed that, conservatives would have been all against it." Cassidy said borrowing money for the payments could put upward pressure on borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards. He instead called for action to reduce the national debt and address Social Security's finances. "We need to actually pay attention to our national debt," Cassidy said. Cassidy also weighed in on reports that Russian billionaire Umar Kremlev paid for portions of Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding celebrations in the Bahamas. The president said Friday that his son had repaid Kremlev. Cassidy, however, said repayment mattered but added that he would like to see it verified. "Anytime someone gives a $250,000 gift, and they have strong ties to the Kremlin, that's wrong," Cassidy said. item.title: State Dept. issues alert to U.S. citizens across the Middle East as tensions rise
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. State Department is seen on Nov. 29, 2010. (Nicholas Kamm/Getty Images) President Donald Trump cut short a weekend stay at Camp David and returned to the White House on Saturday evening, hours after the State Department issued a security alert warning that escalating hostilities in the Middle East could worsen rapidly. Trump arrived at the Ellipse aboard Marine One shortly before 8 p.m., according to the White House press pool. His public schedule had called for him to remain at Camp David until Sunday. War Secretary Pete Hegseth, who visited Texas A&M University Saturday and attended the Aggies' football game against Kentucky, also returned to Washington early. The White House did not immediately explain Trump's early return, which came as the State Department renewed a broad travel warning for Americans in or traveling to the Middle East following renewed attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia. At least 11 U.S. embassies in the region also issued warnings about possible travel disruptions, according to The Associated Press. "Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation," the State Department said in its statement, posted to X on Saturday. The department warned Americans in the region to exercise heightened vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures, and other travel disruptions. The advisory did not urge Americans to leave the region. "Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports," the alert said. "This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly." Americans outside the Middle East were urged to "seriously reconsider travel to and through the region," while those traveling there were advised to closely monitor airport and airline operations. The State Department also said the potential threat extended beyond the Middle East, noting that U.S. diplomatic facilities had been targeted. "Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other U.S. interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including U.S. businesses and other institutions," the alert said. The heightened warning came four days after the State Department updated its travel advisory for Saudi Arabia, which remains at Level 3, "Reconsider Travel." The Sept. 15 advisory cites the risks of Iranian drone and missile attacks against American interests, armed conflict and terrorism. The Saudi advisory says commercial flights remain operational but have faced significant disruptions since hostilities between the United States and Iran began Feb. 28. It also warns that Iranian attacks have targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities, and energy installations throughout Saudi Arabia. The State Department also noted that the Houthis had threatened renewed attacks against Saudi Arabia and warned that falling debris from intercepted missiles and drones posed a risk. Americans living or working near energy infrastructure and military bases could face heightened danger, the advisory said. The warnings followed a Houthi attempt to strike the Saudi capital of Riyadh with a ballistic missile Saturday. Saudi Arabia said the missile was intercepted and no casualties were reported. Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the Yemen-based group launched a "large number of ballistic and cruise missiles" and drones at targets in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh and facilities belonging to state-owned oil giant Saudi Aramco in Yanbu, The Hill reported. The Houthis' claims about attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure could not immediately be independently verified. The attack prompted Riyadh's first air raid alert since renewed Saudi-Houthi fighting began in July, opening another front in the broader Iran war. The U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem also issued a security alert, saying consular services in Jerusalem and at its Tel Aviv branch continued to operate normally while urging Americans to take additional precautions, Israel Hayom reports. The embassy advised U.S. citizens to verify flight status at Ben Gurion and Haifa airports, identify the nearest bomb shelter or safe room, download Israel's Home Front Command app for real-time alerts, and maintain supplies of water, food, and essential medications. item.title: Trump says his planned arch will double as a military complex housing drones and snipers
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump on Sunday said his proposed 250-foot triumphal arch will now be a “top grade” military complex that will house drones, snipers and ammunition, in a social media post that raised new questions about the controversial project. Trump wrote on Truth Social that he has agreed to convert the arch “at the strong request” of the U.S. military, and “for National Security purposes.” Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The “Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” near Arlington National Cemetery will “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage,” Trump wrote. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World.” Trump and his deputies had previously maintained that the arch would be a new tourist attraction, and the administration has released detailed plans of its internal design and outside observation deck. The administration had not previously broached the idea of converting the arch to a military complex, even as the project has undergone months of federally required reviews. The Trump administration plans to begin construction on the arch as soon as November, amid resistance from military veterans, advocacy groups and historic preservationists who say the towering structure will overshadow the nearby cemetery and is too large for the site. A federal judge is weighing whether to halt the project. On Sunday, some critics asked whether the arch would now undergo further required reviews to accommodate Trump’s new vision. “Presumably, this would result in security hardening, inclusive of fencing, guard posts, and other additional features above and beyond what has been approved,” Charles Birnbaum, the CEO of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, wrote in an email to the Commission of Fine Arts, which approved the arch in May. The email was shared with The Washington Post. Critics also questioned the practicality of building a military complex at the center of a widely used traffic circle not far from Reagan National Airport. The White House did not respond to questions about the president’s post, including the need for a military complex at the arch site. The Interior Department, which oversees the federal parkland where the arch would be built, did not reply to requests for comment, and a Pentagon spokesperson said they had nothing to add beyond the president’s post. Trump’s new claims about the arch resemble his arguments for the need to build a ballroom at the White House. Trump initially said the ballroom was needed to entertain guests but more recently has said it was a “desperately needed National Security structure.” That argument also has become central to the administration’s legal claims that the ballroom must be built. Trump has spent nearly a year touting his plans to build an arch at Memorial Circle, a traffic roundabout tucked inside Washington’s boundaries, near the entrance to the military cemetery and managed by the National Park Service. The president and his deputies have said the arch should be built to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary. The administration contends it does not need congressional approval for the arch because lawmakers a century ago authorized a somewhat similar project near the site. “This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X this month. The Trump administration has acknowledged that its arch project will alter pedestrians’ views of the Lincoln Memorial and other historic sites, affect the experience of visiting Arlington National Cemetery and cause other disruptions. A D.C. official last week advised the administration to abandon its plans and instead pursue a less obtrusive alternative. Rep. Don Beyer (D-Virginia), who represents the district that encompasses the cemetery and National Airport, has also urged Trump to stop the project and seek authorization from Congress before building a structure. “Putting a drone launching site directly in the landing path for DCA is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea,” Beyer wrote Sunday, suggesting on X that it was a pretext to strengthen Trump’s legal arguments for the arch. Outside lawyers also questioned Trump’s national security claims. “The President’s belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality,” said Nicolas Sansone, a lawyer at Public Citizen Litigation Group, a watchdog organization that is representing several veterans who say the large arch would alter their experience when visiting the nearby military cemetery. U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan, the Obama administration appointee who is reviewing the veterans’ case, has warned the Trump administration not to abruptly move forward with construction on the arch - as Trump did when demolishing the White House’s East Wing to build his ballroom without seeking approval from federal review panels or from Congress. Trump officials have said they will obtain “all necessary approvals” before beginning construction on the arch. The president’s claim Sunday about the arch being converted to a military complex follows his administration’s evolving legal strategy to defend the ballroom on similar grounds. Administration officials have increasingly contended that the ballroom must be built by citing the planned military complex being constructed underneath it and the need to protect the president. Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, said the administration’s national security claims in the ballroom case had merit. “The equities in this case turn on complex architectural and security determinations best made by the Secret Service and the military - not judges,” Rao wrote in August. Other federal judges have said that Trump could not claim broad national security reasons as a basis to pursue a construction project that had not been authorized by Congress. “While I take seriously the Government’s concerns regarding the safety and security of the White House grounds and the President himself, the existence of a ‘large hole’ beside the White House is, of course, a problem of the President’s own making,” U.S. District Judge Richard Leon - who first blocked work on the ballroom - wrote earlier this year. The Supreme Court on Aug. 31 ruled 5-4 that construction on the ballroom could continue for now but declined to rule on the merits of the administration’s arguments in that case.
